opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a real constraint, but people often frame it the wrong way. The naive version says: we're spending tens of billions, soon hundreds of billions, on compute, and at some point that's a meaningful fraction of GDP and the money just isn't there. That arithmetic is right as far as it goes. You can't keep growing 3x or 5x a year in spending forever against a fixed economy.

The hidden assumption is that the economy stays fixed. The whole bet is that these systems become economically productive, not in a vague "nice chatbot" sense, but doing real work in coding, science, and operations. If that's happening, the revenue grows alongside the spending, and the pie itself starts growing faster. You're not draining a fixed pool; you're investing in something that expands the pool.

So I'd frame it as a race between two curves. One is the cost of the next generation of training and inference. The other is the economic value the models actually generate. If the value curve keeps pace, there's no wall. You hit a wall if capabilities stall, or if they're real but diffuse into the economy too slowly. Diffusion takes time even when the technology is ready. Enterprises have procurement cycles, regulation, and integration work. That gap is where I'd worry.

The other point is that companies like ours have to manage the financial risk carefully. If you overbuild compute on the assumption that revenue shows up on a particular schedule, and it shows up a year late, that can be very painful even if you were right about the long run. Being directionally right but wrong on timing is a real way to get hurt. So I try to be ambitious but not reckless about it.

My overall view: running out of money is a real ceiling if progress stops paying for itself. The evidence so far is that it's paying for itself at a rate that's at least keeping up. I wouldn't call that certain, but I don't think the money runs out before the economic returns arrive.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly calls a fixed economy the hidden assumption behind the argument that compute spending will exhaust available money.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a real question, and I want to take it seriously rather than wave it away, because the numbers are genuinely large. If you extrapolate the current trends, you're talking about hundreds of billions of dollars a year in capex, and at some point people start asking, where does that money come from? Is there enough revenue on the other side to justify it?

The way I think about it is that there are really two separate questions. One is, does the demand exist? And the other is, can the financing keep up with the demand in the short term? And I think the mistake people make is conflating those two.

On the first question, I'm actually quite confident. The reason is that the revenue growth we've seen so far hasn't been driven by hype, it's been driven by the models actually doing things that are worth money to businesses. Coding is the clearest example. A year or two ago, the models could help you with a function. Now they can do substantial chunks of an engineer's job. And when you look at how companies are paying for that, they're paying because it's cheaper than the alternative, which is a human doing the same work. So if you believe the models continue to improve, and I do, then the addressable market isn't some fixed pie of "AI spending," it's a large fraction of the labor economy, which is tens of trillions of dollars. Against that denominator, the compute numbers don't look crazy at all.

The second question is harder, and this is where I think the skeptics have a point. There's a mismatch in timing. You have to build the data centers two or three years before you know for sure the demand will be there. So companies are making bets, and some of those bets could be mistimed. You could have a situation where the demand is real, the technology works, and you still get a bubble-like dynamic because the capital was deployed faster than the revenue showed up. That happened with fiber in the late nineties. The internet was real, the fiber was eventually used, and a lot of companies still went bankrupt.

So my honest view is: I think the fundamental economics are sound, and I think the odds that spending structurally outruns the economy are low, because the thing being produced is substitutable for the most expensive input in the economy, which is human cognitive labor. But I wouldn't rule out a period of overshoot or a correction along the way. Those are different things. One is a question about whether the technology is worth it. The other is a question about whether every individual bet gets the timing right. And I'd be surprised if every bet got the timing right.

r001.rationale: The response argues that AI can address a large labor market and that AI spending is not a fixed pie, but it does not identify the exhaustion argument as assuming the economy remains fixed in size.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two different questions here. One is whether the current rate of growth in compute spending can continue indefinitely. Obviously it can’t. If you extrapolate any sufficiently fast exponential, eventually you get a number that’s larger than the economy. But that doesn’t tell you when the growth stops, or what happens before it does.

The second question is whether the systems generate enough economic value to pay for the next generation. That’s the question that matters. You can’t just look at spending going up and conclude that we run out of money. You have to look at revenue, at how useful the models are, and at how quickly that usefulness turns into something people will pay for.

Now, there’s a real timing issue. You might build a very capable model, but it takes businesses a while to integrate it. Meanwhile, you’ve already committed to the infrastructure. So even if the long-term economic case is strong, you can still get a financing crunch along the way.

I would take that risk seriously. But it’s different from saying there’s some fixed pool of money that AI inevitably exhausts. If the technology substantially increases what the economy can produce, then the pool grows. The uncertainty is how quickly that happens relative to how quickly we’re spending.

r001.rationale: The response rejects the idea that AI inevitably exhausts a fixed pool of money and explains that increased economic production can grow that pool, identifying the fixed-economy assumption behind the argument.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish two claims. One is that compute spending can’t keep growing at its current rate forever. That’s clearly true. Eventually you run into the size of the economy, the amount of power you can build, and the capital people are willing to supply.

The other claim is that we hit those limits before AI generates enough economic value to justify the spending. That’s a much more substantive question. You can’t answer it just by extrapolating the cost curve. You also have to ask what the systems can do and how much people will pay for it.

If capabilities keep improving but the revenue doesn’t materialize, then investment will slow down, potentially very sharply. If the systems become useful enough to generate substantial revenue and increase productivity, then the amount the economy can support grows as well.

So I take the financing constraint seriously. But “this exponential can’t continue forever” doesn’t, by itself, tell you when it stops or what we’ll have built by then.

r001.rationale: The response says AI-driven revenue and productivity could expand what the economy can support, but it does not identify the exhaustion argument as assuming the economy remains fixed in size.
